title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: measuring a difference, reporting a question, weighing a life

questions.prompt: A father has heard of a new evening class and wants to know whether it costs less than the one his son attends now — not by how much, simply whether there is a difference at all. Which question does he ask?

options.text: "Is it any cheaper than the present one?"
"Is it very cheaper than the present one?"
"Is it a lot of cheaper than the present one?"
"Is it much more cheaper than the present one?"

questions.explanation: any is the modifier that measures no step at all: it asks whether the difference exists, which is exactly what the father wants, and it lives in questions and negatives — the statement form of the same idea is it is no cheaper. very is the one word English refuses in front of a comparative, however natural it feels; much and far do that work. a lot is a modifier, but a lot of is the quantifier that goes before a noun, not before an adjective. And much more cheaper doubles the comparative: cheaper already carries the more.

questions.prompt: Two evening centres publish their figures for the year: the one in Sfax enrolled 900 adults, the one in Gabès 300. A journalist writes one sentence about each. Which pair is right?

options.text: Sfax enrolled a third as many adults as Gabès; Gabès enrolled three times as many as Sfax.
Sfax enrolled three times as many adults as Gabès; Gabès enrolled a third as many as Sfax.
Sfax enrolled three times as many adults as Gabès; Gabès enrolled three times fewer than Sfax.
Sfax enrolled three times as much adults as Gabès; Gabès enrolled a third as much as Sfax.

questions.explanation: 900 against 300 is a scale of three to one, so Sfax enrolled three times as many adults as Gabès — and the same scale read backwards makes Gabès a third as many, not three times fewer. That phrase is the trap of the whole structure: English multiplies upwards in times and comes down in fractions, so three times fewer says nothing exact. The pair that opens on a third as many reverses the two towns. And adults can be counted, so the block takes many; much belongs to a noun you cannot count, such as money or time.

questions.prompt: A pupil writing up an interview produces this line: "I asked her how long had she worked there." Her teacher marks one fault in it. Which statement names that fault?

options.text: An indirect question always needs if or whether, so how long must be replaced by whether.
An indirect question is still a question, so the line must end in a question mark and not in a full stop.
An indirect question keeps the present, so had worked must become has worked.
An indirect question keeps the word order of a statement, so had she must become she had.

questions.explanation: Everything in the line is right except the order of two words. An indirect question is folded into a sentence and takes the word order of a statement, subject before verb, so had she becomes she had: I asked her how long she had worked there. if and whether are for a question with no WH word, and this one opens on how long, which is kept. The tense is right as it stands: the reporting verb is in the past, so the present perfect of the original question moves back to the past perfect. And an indirect question is a statement about a question, so it closes on a full stop.

questions.prompt: A pupil is asked to leave out every relative pronoun she is allowed to leave out. (1) "The report which the head teacher wrote was three pages long." (2) "The report, which the head teacher wrote in June, was three pages long." What can she leave out?

options.text: the pronoun of the first sentence only
the pronoun of the second sentence only
the pronoun of both sentences
the pronoun of neither sentence

questions.explanation: Two rules meet here. In the first sentence the clause carries no commas, so it is restrictive, and which is the object of wrote — the subject of the clause is the head teacher — so the pronoun may go: the report the head teacher wrote was three pages long. In the second, the commas make the clause non-restrictive, and a non-restrictive clause never drops its pronoun, whatever job that pronoun does inside it. The test is always the same: ask what follows the pronoun. A verb means it is the subject and must stay; a new subject means it is the object and may go — unless commas have already settled the matter.

questions.prompt: Read this note from a careers adviser. "Habib left school at sixteen with no certificate and took a job in a warehouse. Eight years later he enrolled in an evening course, sat for the same examination and passed it. He now earns rather less than he did in the warehouse, but he answers to nobody and signs his own reports." Which statement does the note support?

options.text: Habib went back to study because the warehouse paid him badly.
Habib earns more today than he did in the warehouse.
Habib gave up part of his pay for a rise in status.
Habib's evening course lasted eight years.

questions.explanation: The note gives two facts about his position today and sets them against each other: he earns rather less, and he answers to nobody and signs his own reports. That is the exchange this module is built on — money given up for a rise in status. The idea that the warehouse paid him badly is turned round by the note itself, since the warehouse paid him more than the job he holds now. The claim that he earns more today is the plain opposite of what is written. And the eight years are the interval between the warehouse and the evening course, not the length of the course.

questions.prompt: The training programme of the module's article lasted between two and three hours, and afterwards the share of pupils doing what the teacher asked reached 94 per cent. A reader concludes: "So praise on its own solves classroom violence." Which of these, printed in the same article, is an objection to his conclusion?

options.text: That the training lasted no more than three hours.
That teachers praise good work far more readily than good behaviour.
That some pupils go on behaving badly however much praise they are given.
That disciplining a child in front of the whole class is the worst thing a teacher can do.

questions.explanation: The union secretary grants that praise motivates and then limits the claim: saying that praise is all a teacher has to do is far too simplistic, because some pupils remain disruptive whatever praise they receive. That is an objection, and it lands exactly on the words on its own. The length of the training is a fact already given in the question and argues neither way. The observation that teachers praise work readily and behaviour rarely comes from the psychologist and supports the article rather than answering it. And the line about disciplining a child in front of the class is the researchers' own argument for the method, so it cannot be an objection to it.
